L7.01.title: Orientation & Baseline: What "Advanced Reader" Means
L7.01.goal: Understand the Level 7 finish line in concrete terms; take a baseline stamina/speed reading; meet the academic-vocabulary routine that runs through the whole level.

prompts: From Level 6: name the 5 expository text structures (sequence, cause/effect, compare/contrast, problem/solution, description) and the 4 reciprocal-teaching roles (predict, question, clarify, summarize). Write them from memory, then check against this list. If you can't recall 3+ of either, review your Level 6 notes before continuing — this level assumes both are automatic.

vocab.def: to work out something not directly stated, using clues plus what you already know
examples: The story never says she was angry, but I infer it from her slammed door.
Detectives infer who committed a crime from evidence, not confessions.
vocab.task: infer something about a neighbor from one clue (a locked gate, a light on at 3am) without being told it directly.

vocab.def: to confirm something using an independent, separate source
examples: One witness says the car was blue; a security camera corroborates it.
A single study rarely proves a drug works — later studies have to corroborate it.
vocab.task: name one thing you believe that is corroborated by more than one source (a news event, a fact from school), and one thing you believe that you've never checked against a second source.

vocab.def: a leaning toward one side, often invisible to the person who has it, that shapes what they notice, report, or leave out
examples: A company's own website has a bias toward praising its own product.
A sports fan's bias makes them see every close call against their team as unfair.
vocab.task: name a source (a person, a website, a channel) whose bias you already account for when you read or listen to it, and say what the bias is.

facts: this level's five "rooms" (history, science, argument, contracts, data) map onto how Shanahan & Shanahan (2008) found real historians, scientists, and other specialists actually read — not a generic invented list (research/06 §1.8).
SHEG's 2019 national study found 96% of students did not check a website's bias before trusting it — the gap this whole level is built to close (research/06 §1.9).
prime.question: which of the five "rooms" do you think you already do some version of, without anyone teaching you — and which feels like a completely new skill?

text.title: The finish line, in a text
paragraphs: What Does It Mean to Read Well?

Ask a six-year-old what a good reader can do, and the answer is simple: read a page without stopping. Ask a hiring manager, a nurse reading a drug interaction chart, or a citizen deciding how to vote, and the answer gets larger and much harder to fake. Real advanced reading is not a single skill; it is a bundle of moves that specialists in different fields learned to make automatic inside their own subject before anyone called it "critical reading" at all.

A historian who opens a soldier's diary from 1770 does not read it the way she reads a modern newspaper. She asks who wrote it, when, and why, before she asks what it says — a soldier defending himself in court writes a different account than a bystander with nothing to lose. She then goes looking for a second, independent account of the same event, because a single voice, however sincere, is a claim, not a fact, until something else corroborates it.

A scientist reading a study asks a different set of questions: what, exactly, was measured; how many people or things were tested; and — the trap that catches almost everyone outside the field — whether two things moving together (say, ice cream sales and drowning deaths, both rising every summer) actually means one causes the other, or whether a hidden third factor (hot weather) is driving both. A journalist reading a company's press release asks who benefits if the reader believes the headline. A tenant reading a lease asks which sentence, buried in paragraph nine, quietly changes what a friendlier sentence in paragraph two seemed to promise.

None of these moves are exotic. They are teachable, and they are largely the same handful of questions — who is speaking, what is their evidence, does something independent confirm it, what would change my mind — asked inside four or five different rooms. Two large research traditions converge on this point from different directions. One (Shanahan & Shanahan, 2008) studied working historians, scientists, and mathematicians and found each discipline reads its own texts in genuinely different, learnable ways, and that generic "read the textbook" strategies stop working for readers once they pass roughly a middle-school level of skill. The other (the Stanford History Education Group's 2019 national study of nearly 3,500 students) found that most people, including capable ones, do not do this automatically online: over half judged a piece of unverified video "strong evidence," two-thirds could not tell a paid advertisement from a news story, and almost nobody checked who was behind a website before trusting it. The gap between those two findings is exactly what an advanced reader closes: not more reading, and not a longer checklist, but the specific, disciplined habit of asking a source what it is and what would confirm or break it, every single time, before believing what it says.

That is the finish line this level is built around: not reading faster, though speed matters, and not reading harder books for their own sake, though the books here are genuinely hard — but reading like the specialist whose room you happen to be standing in, and never fully trusting a single voice until something independent has had a chance to argue with it.
questions: According to the passage, what is the actual difference between how a historian reads a soldier's diary and how she reads a modern newspaper?

Think question: The passage claims specialists' reading habits reduce to "largely the same handful of questions... asked inside four or five different rooms." List those questions in your own words. Do you think the same four questions really would work for reading a poem (Session 13)? Why or why not — answer before you've done that session; you'll revisit this.

discuss.prompt: Which of the five "rooms" (history, science, argument, contracts, data) you expect to find hardest, and why.
Ask one question this passage raised that it doesn't answer.
Find the one sentence in paragraph 5 that states the course's actual thesis, and explain it as if to someone who skipped the passage.
The whole passage in exactly two sentences.

L7.01.write: In 4–6 sentences: pick ONE of the four "rooms" you already do some version of in real life (you compare prices before buying something = data reading; you decide whether to trust a stranger's online review = source credibility) and describe, honestly, one specific time your instinct failed you — a time you believed something you shouldn't have. This is your personal baseline; you'll return to it in Session 14.
check: Give a correct one-sentence definition of infer, corroborate, and bias — 3/3 ✓.

State, without looking, the four questions a specialist reader asks of any source (who's speaking / what's their evidence / does something independent confirm it / what would change my mind) — approximate wording is fine.
State your baseline WPM and one honest example from Section 6.

L7.02.title: Reading Like a Historian I: Sourcing & Contextualizing
L7.02.goal: Learn the historian's first two moves — sourcing (who made this, what's their stake?) and contextualizing (what was happening around this moment?) — using TWO competing visual sources compared against each other, then a written primary source.

vocab.def: a formal, sworn written statement about what someone saw or knows, usually given as part of a legal case
examples: The witness gave a deposition describing the accident.
vocab.task: why might someone's account change between an informal conversation and a sworn deposition?

vocab.def: a firsthand account or original document (or image) from the time and place being studied (a diary, a deposition, a photograph, an engraving, a letter) — as opposed to a secondary source (a textbook or article written later, describing events secondhand)
vocab.task: is a newspaper article written the day after an event a primary or secondary source? (Answer: primary — it's from the time, even though the reporter wasn't necessarily an eyewitness.)

facts: In 1770, Boston was a city of about 16,000 people with roughly 2,000 British soldiers stationed in it — a huge, resented military presence in a small town.

Newspapers and printed images in this period were openly partisan; there was no norm of "neutral reporting" the way there is (in theory) today — a printer picked a side and sold to that side's readers.

A single, chaotic, five-minute event on a dark, snowy street produced dozens of conflicting eyewitness accounts and at least two competing engraved images, made within weeks of each other by rival artists — which is exactly why it is one of the most-used teaching events in American historical-reading instruction (it's the anchor event of the Stanford History Education Group's own "Reading Like a Historian" curriculum, research/06 §1.9).
prime.question: think of a recent event (a sports call, a video that went viral, a local dispute) where you saw two people describe the same five minutes so differently you'd never have known it was the same event without being told. What made their accounts diverge — what each person could actually see, or what each person wanted to be true?

text.title: Background, then three sources (two visual, one written)
paragraphs: Background: In the winter of 1770, British troops had been stationed in Boston for over a year, partly to enforce unpopular taxes. Relations between soldiers and residents were tense — soldiers took off-duty jobs that competed with local workers, and there had been earlier scuffles. On the night of March 5, 1770, a crowd gathered around a small group of British soldiers guarding the customs house on King Street. The crowd grew, shouted insults, and threw snowballs, ice, and oyster shells. In the chaos, the soldiers fired into the crowd. Five colonists died. The soldiers and their commanding officer, Captain Thomas Preston, were arrested and charged with murder — an explosive case, since Boston's Patriot movement wanted the soldiers punished as an example, while the Crown needed a fair trial to avoid a wider uprising. (Patriot lawyer John Adams chose to defend the soldiers, arguing that a lawful trial mattered more than a convenient outcome — Preston and six soldiers were acquitted of murder; two soldiers were convicted of manslaughter. You'll read part of Adams' own closing argument in Session 3.)

Source 1 — a visual source: the best-known engraving of the event, published under the name of Boston silversmith and engraver Paul Revere, roughly three weeks after the massacre (late March 1770). Described in words below rather than reproduced as an image.

The engraving shows a straight line of British soldiers, muskets leveled, firing in an apparently coordinated volley into a small, unarmed, retreating crowd — no one in the crowd is shown holding a weapon, throwing anything, or threatening the soldiers. Captain Preston stands beside his men with his sword raised, in a pose many viewers read as actively signaling the order to fire. Above the customs house, the engraving adds a sign reading "Butcher's Hall" — a building detail invented for the image, not present at the real customs house. A dog stands calmly in the foreground, undisturbed by the "chaos," reinforcing the sense of an orderly execution rather than a riot.

Documented history of this specific image, so the sourcing questions below have a real answer: engraver Henry Pelham had drawn this composition first and privately shown it to Revere, a fellow Boston engraver, before Pelham's own version was printed. Revere copied Pelham's design and rushed his own version into print and onto sale roughly a week before Pelham could sell his original — Pelham wrote Revere an angry letter accusing him of dishonorably stealing an unpublished work and profiting from it under his own name. Revere's version (the one that became famous and widely reprinted) is the one described above.

Source 1b — a second visual source, for direct comparison: Henry Pelham's original composition, "The Fruits of Arbitrary Power, or the Bloody Massacre," advertised for sale April 2, 1770 (about a week after Revere's copy had already gone on sale). Described in words below.

Pelham's original is, by design, the source Revere copied — the overall composition (the soldiers' firing line, Preston with sword raised, the retreating unarmed crowd) is essentially the same scene, since Revere reproduced Pelham's drawing rather than making an independent one. The one substantive difference documented across sources: Revere's printed version adds the "Butcher's Hall" sign over the customs house that is not part of Pelham's original design — Revere's own embellishment on top of the composition he took from Pelham.

Source 2 — Captain Thomas Preston, commanding officer, written from his jail cell and later published in the London Public Advertiser (April 1770). Adapted into modern spelling and condensed from the historical record — see the precise source note at the end of this lesson.

"It is matter of too great notoriety to need any proofs that the arrival of his Majesty's troops in this town was extremely obnoxious to it... On the 5th of March, a party of soldiers was ordered to relieve the sentinel at the customs house. The mob, which had grown to several hundred, pressed upon the soldiers, calling them 'lobster scoundrels' and daring them, 'Fire, if you dare.' They struck the soldiers with clubs and threw pieces of ice. One soldier, struck hard enough to be knocked down, rose and fired his musket. I heard the word 'fire' shouted, but I do not know from whom, and I gave no such order — my own words were, 'Do not fire, stop your firing.' Whether from the crowd's own shout or from confusion in the smoke and noise, several of the men, believing the order had been given, discharged their pieces, not all at once but raggedly, one after another. I take God to witness that I gave no order to fire, and I did all in my power to prevent the very tragedy that followed, being as innocent a sufferer in this affair as it is possible for any man to be."
questions: Who made each image, and when, relative to the event and relative to each other? (Pay attention to who saw whose version first, and who got to print and sell theirs first.)

The one documented difference between them is the "Butcher's Hall" sign. Given that Pelham and Revere otherwise share the same composition, the same firing-line staging, and the same political sympathies, what does it tell you that Revere still chose to add one more detail on top of a design he didn't even originate?

Predict, then check: before reading the description again, what would you expect an image made for these purposes to emphasize about the soldiers and the crowd? Does the actual description match your prediction?
Who wrote this, when (relative to his own trial), and for what purpose?
Preston insists on one specific fact three separate times. What is it, and why would that fact matter more to him than almost anything else in the account?

Direct comparison to Sources 1/1b: both engravings show one coordinated volley on a visible signal from Preston. Source 2 says the shots came "not all at once but raggedly, one after another," with no order given at all. These cannot both be fully accurate. Which source has a clearer, nameable reason to shape the story this particular way — and does that mean the other source is simply "true"? (This is the bridge to Session 3: a document contradicting an image is not automatically the correct one; both need to be weighed.)

Contextualizing check: does knowing Source 2 was written from jail, before a murder trial, change how much weight you give it? Does that mean it's false — or just that it needs an independent source to corroborate or contradict it?

discuss.prompt: Before Session 3's further sources, predict whether an ordinary bystander's account will side with Sources 1/1b's "clear signal, coordinated volley" or Source 2's "no order, ragged shots" — or neither exactly.
What question would you want to ask Revere directly about his choice to add "Butcher's Hall" to a composition he'd copied from Pelham?

Explain, in your own words, why sourcing an image uses the same four questions as sourcing a document, and why comparing two versions of the same image (Pelham vs. Revere) can reveal a bias neither version would show on its own.
Two sentences — what do the visual and written sources agree and disagree on, and what remains unconfirmed?

L7.02.write: Write a short paragraph (5–7 sentences): compare the visual sources (1/1b) and the written source (2) on the one factual question both address (was there a clear order, in one coordinated volley, or not) — name each source's likely bias and what each stood to gain from its version. Use bias and primary source correctly at least once each.
check: Compare your answers with the model answer.

Can you state, without notes, the sourcing template (who/when/why/predict) from memory, and name a specific, concrete bias for the visual sources AND the written one? If you can only name Preston's bias and not the engravers', reread Section 5 before Session 3.

L7.03.title: Reading Like a Historian II: Corroboration
L7.03.goal: Learn the historian's third move — corroboration: reading further independent accounts of the same event, applying the SAME sourcing template to each one (not just the first document you meet), and seeing where accounts agree, disagree, and where the disagreement itself is the most important finding.

prompts: What specific fact did Source 1 (the engraving) and Source 2 (Preston) directly disagree about?

vocab.def: a difference or disagreement between two accounts of the same thing
examples: There was a discrepancy between the two witnesses' description of the getaway car's color.
vocab.task: a discrepancy doesn't automatically mean one person is lying — name another reason two honest witnesses might describe the same event differently (different vantage point, stress, memory, what they were focused on).

vocab.def: a witness who was not just watching but did something during the event themselves (intervened, was struck, struck someone) — as distinct from a purely passive bystander. An involved witness is not automatically less honest, but their own actions can shape, understandably, how they remember and describe what happened next

facts: the real Boston Massacre trial record includes testimony from dozens of witnesses, and historians studying it today still cannot fully reconcile every detail — not because the record is bad, but because five minutes of a violent, dark, snow-covered street scene genuinely looks different from every different position in the crowd.
prime.question: if a fight broke out in a crowded room you were standing in, would you expect your own account afterward to be fully accurate about who moved first — or would adrenaline and your own angle make some details genuinely unreliable, through no dishonesty on your part?

text.title: A third source, sourced first
paragraphs: Source 3 — Richard Palmes, Boston merchant. From his sworn testimony at the soldiers' trial, as transcribed in the trial record (Boston, 1770). Quoted directly, in the original phrasing and spelling, from the primary-source transcription at bostonmassacre.net/trial/d-palmes.htm — see the precise source note below.

"I went to see what was the matter, and found Captain Preston at the head of six or eight soldiers... I asked him if the soldiers' guns were loaded. He answered they were. I asked him if they were going to fire upon the inhabitants. He answered by no means... I had not been there more than two minutes before I heard the word 'fire'... I heard the report of a gun... After that gun went off I heard the word fire, but who said it I know not... After that I turned and saw the Grenadier who fired first, attempting to prick me by the side of the Captain with his bayonet. I had a large stick in my hand. I struck over-hand and hit him on his left arm, and knocked his hand from his gun. Upon that I turned, thinking the other would do the same, and struck at anybody at first, and hit the Captain."
(Palmes also testified the whole encounter, from first shout to last shot, lasted "not more than three quarters of a minute in the whole.")
questions: Who is Palmes, when did he give this account (relative to the trial), and for what purpose was it recorded (sworn trial testimony, not a private diary)?

In his own words, when did Palmes strike the soldier — before, or after, that soldier had already fired? What was Palmes' stated reason for striking him (read the sentence just before "I struck over-hand" again)?

This is the teaching point: other, independent secondary accounts of this same night describe a second detail Palmes' own quoted testimony above doesn't spell out in this much length — that his blow aimed at Captain Preston (the one right after he struck the soldier) narrowly missed Preston's head and landed on his arm instead, by some accounts because Palmes slipped on the icy ground. A witness who was himself swinging a weapon in the final seconds before and after the first shot is describing his own actions, under oath, in a chaotic scene, about facts that bear directly on his own potential legal exposure. What would you check, knowing that, before taking his account of "who fired first" and "why" at face value? (There is no single settled answer here — historians and popular accounts genuinely disagree on some of the finer sequencing; naming that disagreement honestly is the correct move, not picking a version and stating it as fact.)

Does the fact that Palmes physically struck a soldier make him an involved witness rather than a neutral one? Does that automatically make his account less trustworthy than a pure bystander's would be — or does it mean his stake and vantage point are different from Preston's, and need to be weighed on their own terms, the same as any other source?

text.title: How the case was actually decided
paragraphs: Source 4 — from John Adams' closing argument for the defense, given at the soldiers' trial (December 1770), as recorded in the published trial transcript. Quoted directly, checked against the Founders Online Adams Papers transcription — see the precise source note below.
"Facts are stubborn things; and whatever may be our wishes, our inclinations, or the dictates of our passions, they cannot alter the state of facts and evidence."
questions: Who spoke this, when (relative to the trial's outcome), and for what purpose? Adams was a Patriot himself, arguing to acquit British soldiers — why might a Patriot lawyer choose this specific line as his argument's foundation?

Given everything you now know from Sources 1–3 (a propaganda image, an accused officer's defense, and an involved witness's own testimony about his own actions), what do you think Adams meant by "facts... cannot alter the state of facts and evidence" — as a warning against which of the three sources' temptations specifically?

discuss.prompt: If a fifth independent account existed — say, from a soldier standing in the firing line — would you expect it to side more with Source 2/3's uncertainty or Source 1's "clear order" version?
What one question would resolve the discrepancy if you could ask Palmes, Preston, and the engraver Revere directly?

Explain why "Palmes struck a soldier, so ignore his account" would be exactly the wrong move for a historian to make — and why "Palmes' blow caused the shooting" would ALSO be wrong, since his own sworn testimony places his blow after the first shot, not before it.
In two sentences, what does the corroboration of all four sources actually establish, and what remains open?

L7.03.write: Write a short paragraph (6–8 sentences): using the corroboration table, explain what you can now say with confidence about the night of March 5, 1770, what remains uncertain, and why reading Palmes' own testimony directly (rather than a single narrated summary) changed your reading. Use corroborate, discrepancy, and involved witness correctly at least once each.
check: Compare your answers with the model answer.

Fill in the corroboration table correctly (4 rows × 3 sources), correctly state, using Palmes' own quoted words, when his blow landed relative to the first shot and why he says he threw it, and state the real historical trial outcome (Preston and six soldiers acquitted of murder; two soldiers convicted of manslaughter) as an example of how courts, like historians, sometimes have to decide despite real uncertainty.

L7.04.title: Reading a Science Article I: Claim, Method, Sample Size
L7.04.goal: Learn to pull apart a science write-up into its actual claim, the method used to test it, and the sample size — and notice when a headline overstates what the study behind it found.

vocab.def: the specific method a study used: who/what was tested, how, for how long, compared against what
examples: The methodology mattered as much as the result — testing 12 people for one day proves much less than testing 1,200 people for a year.

vocab.def: how many people, animals, or items were actually studied. A small sample can produce a dramatic-looking result by chance; a large sample is much harder to fool
examples: a new study finds
a new study of 14 college students over one weekend finds
vocab.task: which sounds more convincing on its own — "a new study finds"— or "a new study of 14 college students over one weekend finds"? Why does the second version, even though it's the same finding, deserve more skepticism?

vocab.def: before serious scientific journals publish a study, other scientists in the field check the methodology for flaws. It doesn't make a study certainly true, but its absence (an unreviewed press release, a company's own blog post) is a warning sign

facts: most people encounter science not through the original study but through a news headline or company press release written by someone with their own reason to make the finding sound bigger than it is.
a study can be entirely real and still be oversold — the fix is not distrusting all science, it's checking the specific claim against its own method.
prime.question: recall one health or nutrition headline you've seen that turned out, later, to be walked back or contradicted — what do you think went wrong between the real study and the headline?

text.title: The article
paragraphs: Headline: "Blue Light From Phones Wrecks Teen Sleep, New Study Finds"

A study released this month by a wellness startup, GlowGuard, claims that teenagers who use their phones in the hour before bed sleep dramatically worse than those who don't — and the company is using the finding to promote its blue-light-filtering phone case.

Researchers gave 24 volunteers, aged 15–17, from a single private school, a sleep-tracking wristband for one week. For the first three nights, participants used their phones normally before bed. For the next three nights, participants were asked to avoid phone screens for the hour before sleep. The wristbands measured total sleep time and how often each person woke up during the night.

On the "no phone" nights, the average participant fell asleep 9 minutes faster and had 1.2 fewer awakenings than on the "phone" nights. The company's press release states: "GlowGuard's research proves that screen time is the single biggest cause of poor sleep in teenagers today," and recommends its $34 phone case as "the scientifically-proven fix." The release does not mention whether participants were told which nights mattered to the study's hypothesis (which could have changed their behavior or self-reports), whether anything else about their evening routine changed between the two conditions, or whether the effect held for the group's typical teenager, given that all 24 participants attended the same private school and volunteered after seeing a flyer specifically about the study, which may itself attract families already concerned about screen time and sleep.

Outside the press release, a real body of published, peer-reviewed research on blue light, screens, and sleep does exist and does find some effect on falling-asleep time in larger, more carefully controlled studies — but the specific "wrecks" and "single biggest cause" language, the 24-person single-school sample, and the same company's product being sold as the "proven fix," are all reasons to read this particular article's own claim skeptically, even if the underlying general idea (screens before bed can affect sleep) has other, better support elsewhere.
questions: State the article's actual claim (not the headline) in one sentence: what, precisely, changed, by how much, for whom?
What was the method? Name at least two things about the method that are weaker than they'd need to be to support "proves" in the company's own words.

Think question: the article says a real, better-supported body of research on this general topic does exist elsewhere. Why is it important to separate "the general idea might be true" from "this specific press release proves it," even when you suspect the underlying idea has merit? What's the risk of not making that separation?

discuss.prompt: If this study were repeated with 600 teenagers across 20 schools, would you expect the effect to get bigger, smaller, or stay about the same, and why?
What's one question you'd want answered before trusting the "$34 fix" recommendation specifically?
Explain, to someone who only read the headline, why "proves" is too strong a word for what this study actually showed.
Two sentences — claim and one key limitation.

L7.04.write: Write a paragraph (5–7 sentences) rewriting the headline and the first sentence of the article so they accurately reflect the study's actual size and method — without pretending the finding is meaningless. Use methodology and sample size correctly at least once each.
check: Could you name, without rereading, the three questions a scientific reader asks (what was measured / what was the method / how many, and how representative)? Could you separate "the general idea may have real support" from "this article proves it"? If either is shaky, reread Section 5 once.

L7.05.title: Reading a Science Article II: Correlation vs. Causation & Data in Text
L7.05.goal: Tell the difference between "two things happen together" and "one causes the other"; read a percentage, a described graph, or a statistic used inside an argument and judge whether it actually supports the claim built on top of it.

prompts: From memory: what three questions does a scientific reader ask of a study (Session 4)?
What went wrong with the GlowGuard press release specifically?

vocab.def: when two things tend to change together (as one goes up, the other tends to go up or down too)
examples: Correlation

vocab.def: when one thing actually makes the other happen. Establishing causation usually needs a controlled experiment, not just an observed pattern

facts: almost any two things that both rise and fall with the seasons, the economy, or a population's growth will show some correlation, whether or not either one causes the other.
journalists and advertisers both have an incentive to state a correlation as if it were a proven cause, because "X causes Y" is a much more compelling sentence than "X and Y happen to move together."
prime.question: recall a headline you've seen that claimed one thing "causes" another — would "is linked to" have been the more honest word?

text.title: A real, classic example
paragraphs: Ice Cream and Drowning

Every summer, two numbers rise together in most countries with cold winters: ice cream sales and the number of people who drown. Track this across any year and the two lines climb and fall in almost the same shape, month by month. If you only looked at the correlation, you could write a headline: "Ice Cream Sales Linked to Drowning Deaths" — and it would be, strictly, true: the two numbers do correlate.

Nobody seriously believes ice cream causes drowning, or that drowning makes people crave ice cream. The real explanation is a confounding variable: hot weather. Hot weather makes people buy more ice cream, and hot weather also makes far more people go swimming — which is when almost all drownings happen. Ice cream and drowning are correlated only because they share a common cause; neither one causes the other at all.

This example is famous precisely because it's obvious once explained — which is exactly why it's useful. The same structure hides inside far less obvious, far more consequential claims: a study might find that people who take a particular vitamin have fewer heart attacks, and a headline might imply the vitamin protects the heart — when the real explanation could be that people who already exercise, don't smoke, and see a doctor regularly are more likely to take vitamins in the first place, and it's the exercise and non-smoking doing the protective work, not the pill.
questions: Think question: the passage says this "hides inside far less obvious... claims." Why is an obvious example like ice cream/drowning actually more useful for learning the pattern than a realistic-but-murky one would be on its own?

text.title: Data in text
paragraphs: A local news segment reports: "Since the new speed cameras went up on Elm Street last year, accidents are down 40%! Clearly the cameras are working." What the segment does not mention: Elm Street also had a new stop sign installed the same month, a nearby school closed (cutting morning traffic by roughly a third), and the city-wide accident rate — across streets with no cameras at all — also fell about 25% that year, likely due to a mild winter with less ice.
questions: What is the segment's causal claim, and what's the correlation it's actually built on?

Given the city-wide 25% drop with no cameras anywhere, roughly how much of Elm Street's 40% drop might the cameras actually explain — all of it, none of it, or something in between? Defend your estimate using the numbers given.

discuss.prompt: Name one confounding variable you'd want ruled out before believing a claim like kids who play chess get better grades.
What's one real headline you've seen that you now suspect confuses correlation with causation?
Explain the difference between "correlation" and "causation" to someone who's never heard either word.
Two sentences on the speed camera example.

L7.05.write: Write a paragraph (5–7 sentences): pick either the ice-cream/drowning or speed-camera example and explain what would need to be true for the causal claim to actually be well-supported (e.g., a controlled trial: cameras installed on some streets and not others, similar in every other way, compared over the same period). Use correlation, causation, and confounding variable correctly at least once each.
check: Compare your answers with the model answer.
Can you correctly identify the confounding variable in both examples without rereading, and explain in one sentence why "correlation" alone never proves "causation"?

L7.06.title: Reading an Argumentative Essay: Claim, Reasons, Evidence, Counterargument
L7.06.goal: Map an op-ed into its working parts — the claim, the reasons given, the evidence behind each reason, and whether it engages a real counterargument or dodges one.

vocab.def: the main position an argument is trying to convince you of. Everything else in the essay should serve the claim
the strongest opposing view, stated fairly, before the writer responds to it. A writer who never mentions the other side's best point is either unaware of it or hiding it from you
the writer's specific response to the counterargument — not just repeating the original claim louder, but actually answering the opposing point

facts: an op-ed's job is to persuade, not to present both sides equally — that's not dishonest by itself, but it means a reader has to do the "both sides" work that the writer isn't obligated to do.
the strongest persuasive essays usually name the best opposing argument themselves, because ignoring it looks worse than answering it.
prime.question: think of a real school or family rule you've disagreed with — what would the single strongest argument FOR that rule be, even though you don't agree with it?

text.title: The op-ed
paragraphs: Schools Should Ban Phones During the School Day — All Day, Not Just in Class

Last month, our district's school board considered banning phones only during class time, letting students use them freely at lunch and between periods. That policy doesn't go far enough. Schools should ban phones for the entire school day, and the case for doing so is stronger than most parents realize.

First, the evidence on attention is not close. A 2023 U.K. review of dozens of studies on phone use and student attention (cited by that country's Department for Education in its own guidance) found that even having a phone visible on a desk — turned off, screen down — measurably reduces performance on attention-demanding tasks, because part of the brain keeps tracking the phone's presence. A partial ban that allows phones at lunch means the phone is back in every student's pocket, and back on every student's mind, minutes before the next class starts.

Second, the case isn't only about attention in class — it's about what actually happens during unstructured time. Lunch and passing periods used to be when students practiced exactly the skills a phone lets them avoid: starting a conversation with someone new, sitting with discomfort instead of reaching for a screen, resolving a small disagreement face to face. Several districts that moved to all-day bans (not just in-class bans) reported, in follow-up surveys of teachers and staff, a rise in students eating lunch together in conversation rather than each alone on a phone — a change that a partial, in-class-only ban did not produce, because the phone was still available the moment class ended.

Opponents raise a real concern: parents want to be able to reach their child quickly in an emergency, and a full-day ban makes that harder. This is the strongest argument against an all-day policy, and it deserves a real answer, not dismissal. The answer most all-day-ban districts have used is a single, clearly communicated exception: the school office remains reachable by phone at all times, and in a genuine emergency, staff can reach any student in minutes — faster, in practice, than a parent could reach a distracted teenager glancing at a notification between classes. A full ban paired with a reliable office-contact system protects the one legitimate use case (real emergencies) without preserving the everyday use (texting friends at lunch) that the emergency argument was never really about.

A partial, in-class-only ban treats the problem as being about classroom instruction time alone. The stronger, better-supported case is that a phone in a student's pocket at all changes what that student does with every unscheduled minute of the day — which is exactly the time schools should be protecting, not just the fifty minutes of class.
questions: What counterargument does the essay name, and does it actually answer it, or just acknowledge it and move on? Quote the sentence that does the actual answering.

Think question: the essay's second reason relies on "several districts... reported, in follow-up surveys" — how strong is that evidence compared to the first reason's cited review of "dozens of studies"? Does the essay treat both reasons as equally certain, or is one clearly weaker — and should the writer have said so?

discuss.prompt: What's the strongest counterargument the essay does NOT address (hint: think about students with medical conditions who need phone-based apps, or working teens who need to coordinate rides)?
What evidence, if it existed, would most weaken the essay's claim?
Explain the difference between a reason and evidence using this essay.
State the essay's argument as a simple because-therefore chain in two sentences.

L7.06.write: Write a paragraph (6–8 sentences) mapping the essay: claim, reason 1 + its evidence, reason 2 + its evidence, the counterargument named, and whether the rebuttal actually answers it. End with your own one-sentence judgment: is this a well-supported argument, a partially-supported one, or weak — and why. Use claim, counterargument, and rebuttal correctly at least once each.
check: Could you list claim/2 reasons/evidence-for-each/counterargument/rebuttal without rereading? Did you correctly judge reason 2's evidence as weaker than reason 1's?

L7.07.title: Argument Evaluation: Logical Fallacies & Evidence Strength
L7.07.goal: Name six common logical fallacies and spot them in a real-feeling argument; rank evidence from strong to weak inside one essay.

prompts: From memory: what are the four parts of an argument map (Session 6)?
What made Reason 2 in the phone-ban essay weaker than Reason 1?

vocab.def: misrepresenting an opponent's argument as weaker or more extreme than it really is, then attacking that weak version
examples: She wants some gun regulations, so he says: 'My opponent wants to take away everyone's guns' — that's not what she said.

vocab.def: attacking the person making an argument instead of the argument itself
examples: You can't trust his climate research, he drives a big truck.

vocab.def: presenting only two options when more exist
examples: Either we ban phones completely, or we let chaos reign

vocab.def: claiming one step will inevitably lead to an extreme, unlikely chain of consequences, without evidence for each link
examples: If we allow a four-day school week, next they'll cancel school altogether.

vocab.def: claiming something is true or right because many people believe it
examples: Millions of people take this supplement, so it must work.

vocab.def: citing an authority who is not actually an expert on the specific claim, or overstating consensus
examples: A famous actor says this diet works

facts: logical fallacies have been catalogued and named since ancient Greek philosophy because the same handful of flawed-reasoning patterns keep working on audiences, century after century.
a fallacy-filled argument can still have a true conclusion — the fallacies are a flaw in how the case is made, not automatic proof the underlying claim is false.
prime.question: recall an ad, speech, or argument that felt convincing in the moment but that you couldn't fully explain why, afterward — what might have been doing the persuading?

text.title: The op-ed
paragraphs: The Four-Day School Week Is Overdue
Districts nationwide are experimenting with four-day school weeks, and it's time more of them did. The case is straightforward, and the objections don't hold up under any real scrutiny.

Teachers everywhere are exhausted, and morale surveys from four-day districts consistently show higher teacher satisfaction and lower turnover than comparable five-day districts. A district superintendent in Colorado, who switched three years ago, put it simply: "Our teachers are happier and we're keeping more of them" — and honestly, if it's good enough for a superintendent who's actually run the experiment, that should settle the question for any parent still on the fence.

Critics say a four-day week hurts learning. But look at what's really being proposed here: some opponents act as though switching to four days means cutting a fifth of all instruction time entirely, as if the missing day simply vanishes into nothing — when in reality, most four-day districts extend the remaining four days by 45–60 minutes each, recovering most of the lost hours. The people attacking this policy the loudest, incidentally, tend to be the same superintendents who resisted remote learning changes during the pandemic and were proven wrong then too — so their objections here deserve the same skepticism.

And consider where this goes if we don't act: districts that refuse to modernize their schedules risk losing teachers to four-day neighbors first, then losing families who move district lines for a better schedule, and eventually risk collapsing entirely as enrollment drains away. The only real question left is whether your district moves now, while it can still choose the timing, or waits and has the decision forced on it later.

Either we adapt the school week to how families and teachers actually live today, or we keep pretending the traditional five-day model is untouchable — and given everything above, that's not really a choice at all.
questions: The superintendent quote ("that should settle the question for any parent") is which fallacy, and why is a single superintendent's opinion weak evidence on this specific list's ranking (Section 4), even though it's not necessarily false?

Think question: the essay's actual factual point about schedule extension ("most four-day districts extend the remaining four days by 45–60 minutes") is a real, checkable claim that could be true. Does finding five fallacies in an essay mean its underlying claim is false? What should a careful reader actually conclude — about this specific essay, and about the general four-day-week question?

discuss.prompt: If you removed every fallacy from this essay and rewrote it using only its one solid, checkable claim (the schedule-extension point) plus real morale-survey data, would it be a weaker or a stronger argument overall?
What evidence would you need to see before believing four-day weeks don't hurt learning outcomes?
Explain the difference between "this essay commits fallacies" and "this essay's conclusion is wrong" to someone who thinks they mean the same thing.
Two sentences: name the essay's one strongest point and its biggest weakness.

L7.07.write: Write a paragraph (6–8 sentences) naming three fallacies you found (name the fallacy + quote it), then state, separately, what a genuinely strong version of this argument would need (e.g., actual outcome data — test scores, graduation rates — from real four-day districts compared to similar five-day ones, not survey satisfaction alone). Use fallacy and one specific fallacy name correctly.
check: Compare your answers with the model answer.
Could you correctly identify at least 4 of 6 fallacies with the right quote, and could you separate "fallacious argument" from "false conclusion" in Q6/the discussion Clarify step?

L7.08.title: Lateral Reading & Source Credibility
L7.08.goal: Practice the single most important habit found missing in the Stanford History Education Group's national study of student online reasoning: actually leaving the page to check who's behind it, on a real organization, before trusting what it says — not just reasoning about it in the abstract.

prompts: From memory: name three of the six fallacies from Session 7.

vocab.def: instead of staying on a webpage and judging it only by how it looks ("vertical" reading, top to bottom), you open new tabs to check who runs the site, what other sources say about it, and whether it's known for accuracy — before deciding whether to trust what's on the page

worthy of belief because of a track record of accuracy, transparency about sources, and accountability for errors. Credibility is earned by an organization or person over time, not claimed by a confident tone
a hidden or undisclosed financial or personal stake that could bias an organization's or person's conclusions, even if every individual fact they state is technically accurate

facts: in SHEG's 2019 national study of nearly 3,500 U.S. students, 96% did not factor a website's bias into whether they trusted it, and most never left the page at all to check (research/06 §1.9). Today you will physically do the thing that study found almost no one does by default.
prime.question: think of the last time you searched for health, product, or nutrition information online — did you check who ran the site you landed on, or just read what it said?

text.title: Lateral-read two real organizations
paragraphs: Do this for real, right now, with a device. You are going to check two real, currently active organizations that regularly publish claims about health, food, and chemical safety. Do not read about them below first — search each one cold, the way you would if you'd landed on their content by accident.
Target A — search: "American Council on Science and Health" funding

Open a new tab. Search that exact phrase. Skim the first several results (not just the organization's own site) and note: who founded it, what topics it covers, and what independent sources (news investigations, watchdog sites, media-literacy organizations) say about its funding.
Target B — search: "FactCheck.org" about funding
Open a new tab. Search that. Note: what organization runs it, how it's funded, and what independent media-bias/media-literacy raters say about its reliability.
Now answer, using what you actually found:
questions: For Target A: name the organization that founded it and at least one type of industry (food/beverage, chemical, pharmaceutical, tobacco) that independent reporting says has funded it. Does the organization's own website disclose this as prominently as the independent reporting does?

Think question: Target A's own homepage does not read as obviously biased — no dramatic claims, no "buy our supplement" link. Why is "the page itself looks neutral" not enough, on its own, to establish credibility — and what did leaving the page actually add that staying on it never would have?

text.title: Expected findings (read after you search)
paragraphs: Target A (American Council on Science and Health): independent reporting — most notably a 2013 Mother Jones investigation based on leaked internal documents, plus watchdog summaries at SourceWatch and DeSmog, and Wikipedia's own sourced funding section — documents that ACSH has received substantial funding over the years from food, beverage, chemical, and pharmaceutical companies (reporting names Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, and chemical/oil firms among past donors), while publicly presenting itself as an independent science-advocacy nonprofit and, per reporting, having stopped disclosing its donor list. Media Bias/Fact Check and similar raters flag it for a strong pro-industry lean on food and chemical safety topics specifically.

Target B (FactCheck.org): it is a project of the Annenberg Public Policy Center at the University of Pennsylvania, funded by an endowment, and its own stated policy is that it does not accept funding from corporations, unions, political parties, or advocacy groups. Independent media-bias raters (e.g., AllSides) generally rate it as nonpartisan/high on factual reporting.

Neither organization is being singled out arbitrarily — both are real, current, and this exact funding information is publicly documented by independent journalism and watchdog sources, not by either organization's opponents alone (see the pinned source note below).

discuss.prompt: If you searched a claim from Target A on a specific food-safety topic, what would you now expect an independent scientific source.
What one piece of information, if Target A's homepage included it, would most change how you read its content?
Explain lateral reading to someone who has never heard the term, using what you just did with Targets A and B as the example.
State which of the two you'd trust more on a contested claim and the single strongest reason why, citing your actual search.

L7.08.write: Write a paragraph (5–7 sentences): describe what you found searching Target A and Target B, and what changed between your first impression (reading each site's own "About" section) and your lateral-read impression (reading independent sources about them). Use lateral reading and conflict of interest correctly at least once each.
check: Compare your answers with the model answer.

Could you name all three lateral-reading questions from memory, and state, using your own actual search results (not a guess), one specific independent source for each organization's funding/reliability reputation?

L7.09.title: Reading a Contract, Policy, or Terms of Service
L7.09.goal: Read a lease and an app's terms of service closely enough to state what you're actually agreeing to, what conditions apply, and what's buried in the fine print.

prompts: From memory: state the three lateral-reading questions (Session 8).

vocab.def: something you are required to do under the agreement (pay rent by the 1st; give 30 days' notice)

one specific section or provision of a contract, usually addressing one issue. Contracts are read clause by clause, not as one flowing paragraph — a single clause can override the general impression given elsewhere in the document
to voluntarily give up a right you would otherwise have
examples: By signing, you waive your right to a jury trial and agree to arbitration instead

facts: surveys of internet users consistently find almost no one reads a terms-of-service document in full before clicking "agree" — the length and legal language are part of the design, not an accident.
a contract's friendliest-sounding sentence and its most restrictive clause can both be true at once — reading only the friendly parts is exactly how the restrictive parts go unnoticed.
prime.question: name one real contract, lease, or terms-of-service agreement you've clicked "agree" to or signed without reading in full.

text.title: A lease excerpt
paragraphs: Excerpt — Residential Lease Agreement
§2. Term. This lease begins June 1 and ends May 31 of the following year (the "Term"). Tenant may not terminate this lease early except as provided in §7.

§4. Rent and Late Fees. Rent is due on the 1st of each month. A payment is considered late if received after 5:00 PM on the 3rd of the month, regardless of postmark date or date sent. A late fee of $75 plus $10 per additional day applies to any late payment. Two late payments within any six-month period constitute a material breach of this lease.

§6. Security Deposit. Tenant's security deposit of one month's rent will be returned within 30 days of move-out, less deductions for damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid rent, or cleaning fees. "Normal wear and tear" does not include, and will result in deductions for: carpet stains of any kind, nail holes larger than a standard picture hook, or any repainting required to restore walls to their original color.

§7. Early Termination. Tenant may terminate this lease before the end of the Term only by (a) providing 60 days' written notice, AND (b) paying an early termination fee equal to two months' rent, AND (c) the unit being successfully re-rented to a new tenant approved by Landlord — until all three conditions are met, Tenant remains responsible for rent.

§11. Dispute Resolution. Any dispute arising under this lease shall be resolved through binding arbitration rather than in court, and Tenant waives the right to a jury trial or to participate in a class action related to this lease.
questions: If rent is due on the 1st, and a tenant mails a check on the 1st that arrives and is processed on the 4th, is that payment late under §4? Quote the exact phrase that answers this.

A tenant assumes "normal wear and tear" covers minor scuffed paint after a year of living there. Does §6 actually agree? Quote the clause and explain the gap between the tenant's assumption and the actual text.

A tenant wants to move out 90 days early because of a new job in another city. List, in order, every condition from §7 that must ALL be true before the lease is actually terminated — is giving 60 days' notice, by itself, enough?
What right does §11 make the tenant waive? Why might someone sign this without realizing they gave up that specific right — what makes this kind of clause easy to skim past?

text.title: A phone app's terms of service excerpt
paragraphs: Excerpt — MoodTrack App Terms of Service

By creating an account, you grant MoodTrack a worldwide, royalty-free, perpetual license to use, reproduce, and create derivative works from any content you submit, including journal entries and mood data, for the purposes of operating, improving, and marketing the Service, including use of anonymized or aggregated data by third-party partners. You may request account deletion at any time; deletion removes your account from active use but anonymized or aggregated data derived from your content prior to deletion may be retained indefinitely.
questions: In plain language, what is the user actually agreeing to let the company do with their private journal entries?
The passage says you can "request account deletion at any time" — does that mean all your data is deleted? Quote the exact phrase that limits this.

discuss.prompt: Which single clause, across both documents, would surprise most people who signed without reading closely?
What question would you ask a landlord or a company directly before signing, based on what you found?
Explain "waive" using the arbitration clause as the example.
In two sentences, state the biggest gap between what each document sounds like at a glance and what it actually says.

L7.09.write: Write a paragraph (6–8 sentences): pick the lease OR the app terms, and explain, as if to a friend about to sign, the two things they most need to know that aren't obvious from a casual read. Use obligation, clause, and waive correctly at least once each.
check: Compare your answers with the model answer.
Could you answer Q1, Q3, and Q6 correctly without rereading the source text? These three are the ones most people get wrong on a first, casual read.

L7.10.title: Synthesis I: Two Sources, Contrasting Viewpoints
L7.10.goal: Combine two opposing op-eds into one written answer that represents both sides fairly and states, specifically, where they actually disagree — not just "some people think X, others think Y."

prompts: From memory: state the four obligations/checks a careful contract reader applies (Session 9).

vocab.def: combining information or viewpoints from more than one source into a new, coherent understanding — not just summarizing each one separately, side by side, and stopping
describing an opposing view the way its strongest supporter would recognize it, even if you disagree with it — the opposite of a straw man (Session 7)
the specific claim, fact, or value judgment where two sources actually part ways — as distinct from things they agree on, or issues neither addresses

facts: two well-argued essays on the same question often agree on more than they disagree on — the disagreement is usually narrower and more specific than "they disagree about phones" suggests.
representing an opposing view fairly is a skill separate from agreeing with it; a strong thinker can state the other side's best point better than a weak thinker can state their own side's.
prime.question: recall a real disagreement (with a parent, friend, or in the news) where, once you stated the other person's actual point instead of your assumption of it, the disagreement turned out to be narrower than you'd thought.

text.title: Two op-eds on the same question
paragraphs: A Full-Day Phone Ban Goes Too Far

Nobody disputes that phones distract students during class — the attention research on that point is genuinely strong, and no serious opponent of a full-day ban argues students should be texting during a lesson. The real disagreement is narrower than full-day-ban advocates suggest: should phones also be banned during lunch and passing periods, when class isn't happening at all?

A full-day ban treats a fifteen-year-old checking a message from a working parent, or coordinating a ride home, the same as a student ignoring a teacher mid-lesson — as if all phone use, everywhere in the building, is equally harmful. It isn't. The in-class case is about protecting instructional time from a specific, measurable distraction. The lunch-period case is about something much softer and less measurable: a hoped-for increase in face-to-face conversation, based on informal staff impressions in a handful of districts, not the kind of large, controlled research that backs the in-class case.

There's also a real equity dimension full-day-ban advocates rarely address directly: students who work part-time jobs, who care for younger siblings after school, or whose parents' work schedules are unpredictable, use lunchtime phone access to coordinate real logistics — a ride, a shift change, a sibling pickup — not just social messaging. A full ban's "office stays reachable" answer assumes every urgent need is an emergency the office would even know to relay; a text about a changed pickup time is not an emergency, but it's still something a student needs to handle, and an office switchboard is a poor substitute for a two-line text a student can send in ten seconds between classes.

None of this means "no phone policy at all." A ban on phone use during instructional time, strictly enforced, addresses the actual, well-evidenced problem. Extending that ban into every unstructured minute of the day trades a strong, specific case for a much weaker, more speculative one — and does it by treating every student's non-class phone use as equally disposable, which for some students, it simply isn't.
questions: What do both essays agree on? Quote the sentence(s) that show the agreement most clearly.
Is the disagreement mainly factual, values-based, or about priorities? Defend your answer using both texts' actual content.
This essay raises an argument the original essay never addressed at all (not just answered weakly — never mentioned). What is it?

Think question: both essays agree the in-class attention research is strong. Given that, what's the actual, narrower question a school board would need to decide — and what additional evidence (not yet in either essay) would help settle it?

discuss.prompt: Which essay's evidence, overall, is stronger on the specific disagreement point (lunch/passing periods), and why?
What data would you want a district to collect before deciding?
Explain "represent fairly" using this second essay's fair treatment of the first essay's strongest point as the example.
Two sentences: agreement, then the actual disagreement.

L7.10.write: Write a synthesis paragraph (7–10 sentences) that: states what both essays agree on; states the specific, narrow point of disagreement; names what kind of disagreement it is; represents each side's strongest point fairly (in your own words, not a straw man); and ends with your own reasoned judgment — which you should be able to defend by naming the specific evidence that moved you, not just a preference. Use synthesis and point of disagreement correctly at least once each.
check: Does your Write to read answer state the specific disagreement (scope: in-class only vs. all-day) rather than a vague "some people disagree about phones"? Did you name the unaddressed equity point?

L7.11.title: Synthesis II: 3–4 Sources, One Research Question
L7.11.goal: The capstone disciplinary-reading task — read four mixed-genre sources (a data summary, a historical document excerpt, a science-style study summary, and an op-ed) on one real question, apply the right discipline-specific move to each, and synthesize all four into one answer. This is PIAAC Level 4–5 territory: "search/integrate/evaluate across multiple dense texts... construct syntheses of similar/contrasting viewpoints" (research/06 §1.11).

prompts: From memory: what four steps does synthesizing two sources require (Session 10)?

vocab.def: to check a claim against three (or more) different kinds of evidence, from independent angles, the way a surveyor fixes a location using three reference points. Today you'll triangulate across four sources of very different kinds

not every source deserves equal trust; a reader has to judge how much each source should count based on what it actually is (see Session 4's evidence-strength ranking) and factor that into the final synthesis

facts: questions like "should companies require full-time office work" rarely have one clean, fully-settled answer — the honest task is weighing real, imperfect evidence of different kinds, not finding the one source that "wins."
the strongest professional writing on hard questions (a policy memo, a board recommendation) routinely synthesizes exactly this mix of data, historical pattern, controlled research, and opinion.
prime.question: think of a real decision in your own life (a job, a purchase, a move) where you had to weigh a personal survey-of-friends kind of evidence against something more rigorous (a review, a data sheet) — which one did you actually trust more, and why?

text.title: Read all four sources, applying the discipline-specific move you learned for each
paragraphs: Source 1 — Data summary (apply Session 5's data-in-text move)

A 2024 survey of 3,200 employees across 40 mid-size U.S. companies that had shifted to hybrid (2–3 office days/week) found: 71% reported preferring hybrid to full-time office work; 58% said they would consider leaving their job if required back full-time; managers at the same companies reported mixed views on productivity — 34% said team productivity had improved under hybrid, 29% said it had declined, and 37% reported no clear change. The survey did not measure actual output data (sales, project completion rates) directly — all productivity figures are manager perception, not measured performance.
Source 2 — Historical context excerpt (apply Session 2–3's sourcing/contextualizing move)

From a 1962 internal memo, a mid-size insurance company, on why the firm was moving from a six-day to a five-day office week (adapted, illustrative period document): "Several of our competitors have adopted the five-day week this year, citing improved morale and no measurable loss in output. We have reviewed our own production figures for the departments that piloted the change last quarter and found output essentially unchanged, with a modest improvement in absenteeism. The Board has therefore approved the five-day week for all departments effective January."

Context note: the standard five-day office week was itself a contested, gradually adopted change in the mid-20th century, resisted at first by many employers on exactly the same "productivity will suffer" grounds now used against hybrid/remote work — worth noting as historical pattern, not proof about today's specific question.
Source 3 — Science-style study summary (apply Session 4's claim/method/sample move)

A frequently cited 2015 workplace study (Bloom, Liang, Ouyang & Ying, published research on a Chinese travel-booking company) had customer-service employees volunteer to work from home for nine months, randomly assigning half to work from home and half to stay in the office —a real controlled experiment, not just an observed pattern. Home workers showed a 13% performance increase (more calls handled per shift), attributed mainly to a quieter environment and fewer sick days; however, home workers were also promoted at roughly half the rate of office workers over the same period, and after the experiment, many home workers voluntarily chose to return to the office, citing loneliness. This is a real, controlled, published, widely-cited study — but it studied one company, one job type (customer service), in one country, in 2015; whether its findings generalize to other kinds of work, or to today's post-pandemic environment, is a real, open question.
Source 4 — Op-ed (apply Session 6–7's claim/reasons/evidence/fallacy move)

"The office isn't just a place to do tasks — it's where junior employees learn by watching how senior colleagues handle a hard client call, where a hallway conversation solves a problem that would have taken a week of scheduled video calls, and where a company's culture actually gets transmitted, not just described in a handbook. Every company that has fully abandoned the office is going to regret it within five years, when they realize they've raised a generation of employees who never learned the informal skills that only come from being physically present. Some hybrid advocates point to survey data showing employees prefer flexibility — but employee preference for an easier arrangement isn't the same as that arrangement being good for their long-term careers, any more than students preferring no homework means no homework is good for their education."

discuss.prompt: Weight the evidence: rank the four sources by evidence strength for the specific question asked, using Session 4's ranking (controlled experiment > survey/observational > single opinion, etc.). Which source is the strongest evidence, and why? Which is the weakest?
Find the real agreement: what does Source 1's data and Source 3's study actually agree on (hint: look at what happened to absences/sick days and performance metrics in both)?

Find the real disagreement/gap: Source 3 found a performance increase for home workers, but also a promotion penalty and eventual voluntary return. Does Source 1's survey measure either of those two things? What does that gap tell you about how much Source 1 alone can settle the question?

Fallacy check (Session 7): Source 4 contains a comparison in its last sentence ("any more than students preferring no homework means no homework is good for their education"). Is this a fair analogy or a weak one? Does it commit a fallacy, and if so which one?
What additional source (a fifth one) would most improve this synthesis — what's the single biggest gap in the evidence as it stands?
What would you ask a company that claims hybrid work hurt productivity, based on Source 1's own limitation?
Explain to someone why Source 3, despite being the strongest single piece of evidence, still can't fully answer the research question alone.
State the synthesis in three sentences.

check: Does your Q6 synthesis name a specific piece of evidence for each claim it makes, rather than a general impression? Did you correctly flag Source 4's analogy as an assumption rather than proof?

L7.12.title: Literary Reading I: Figurative Language, Tone, and Irony
L7.12.goal: Read a short story for what it means beyond its literal events — figurative language, the writer's tone, and irony (when what happens is the opposite of what's expected, or what a character believes is the opposite of what's true).

prompts: From memory: what four things does a synthesis need to do well (Session 10–11)?

vocab.def: language that means something beyond its literal words: metaphor ("her heart was a locked door"), simile ("grief hit like a wave"), personification (giving human qualities to something non-human:
examples: her heart was a locked door
grief hit like a wave

vocab.def: the writer's attitude toward the subject, created through word choice, sentence length, and detail — not what happens, but how the telling feels (cold, warm, mocking, tender, detached)
when the actual outcome of events is the opposite of what was expected or intended — different from sarcasm (a tone of voice) or coincidence (chance, without the reversal-of-expectation element)

facts: literary writers plant details early that only mean something once the ending recontextualizes them — a first read and a second read of the same story are genuinely different experiences.

tone is created by hundreds of small word choices working together, not one obvious signal — which is why two readers can disagree about a story's tone and both be defensible if they can point to real textual evidence.
prime.question: recall a movie, show, or book ending that changed how you understood something from earlier in the story — what detail, looked at again, had been quietly pointing at the twist the whole time?

text.title: An original short story
paragraphs: The Spare Key

Mrs. Aldana kept a spare key to her daughter's apartment on a hook by the door, the way some people keep a fire extinguisher — a thing you own for an emergency you hope never comes, and check, now and then, just to be sure it's still there.

For eleven years the key hung untouched, gathering the particular dust of things nobody expects to need. Her daughter, Renata, called on Sundays, visited at Christmas, sent photographs of a life that looked, from the outside, entirely full — a husband, two children, a kitchen with a window over the sink where the light came in gold in the evenings. Mrs. Aldana kept the photographs on the refrigerator, a small gallery of a life she was allowed to watch but not, she understood, to enter uninvited.

Then, on a Tuesday in March, the telephone did not ring at its usual Sunday hour, and did not ring the Sunday after, and on the third silent Sunday Mrs. Aldana took the spare key down from its hook, feeling the strange lightness of a thing finally doing the job it had waited eleven years to do, and drove the four hours to her daughter's building with her heart performing something between a drumroll and a funeral march.

She let herself in expecting — she would later find it hard to say exactly what she had expected; her mind, in the car, had built entire wings of a house out of silence alone. What she found instead was her daughter at the kitchen table, very much alive, surrounded by paint swatches and takeout containers, in the middle of repainting the same golden kitchen a soft, deliberate blue, three weeks into a separation from her husband that she had not yet found the right sentence to explain over the phone.
"You still have the key," Renata said, not quite a question, looking at the small brass shape in her mother's hand as if it were a photograph of someone she used to be.
"I kept it on the hook by the door," Mrs. Aldana said. "I check that it's still there. I never thought I'd actually need to use it."

Renata almost laughed, the particular laugh of someone catching, for the first time, the shape of an old joke on herself. All those years, she had been the one performing a full life for the refrigerator gallery, careful to send only the golden-kitchen photographs and never the empty Tuesday evenings — and the one emergency the spare key had finally answered was not the catastrophe her mother's silence-built house had imagined, but her own quiet, unphotographed unraveling, three weeks along, that no phone call had yet found the courage to admit.
questions: What is the story's tone toward Mrs. Aldana? Toward Renata? Are they the same, and what specific word choices tell you?
State the situational irony at the story's center: what did the spare key's use turn out to be for, versus what eleven years of keeping it had prepared Mrs. Aldana to expect?

Think question: the story never states directly that Renata had been hiding her real life from her mother — it's built entirely from inference (Session 1's word). What specific details let you infer this, and how does the ending's irony depend on that inference being correct?

discuss.prompt: Before you reread, what might a reader expect to find behind that apartment door, given the buildup in paragraph 3 — and is the actual discovery better or worse than that expectation, and for whom?
What one detail would you want to know that the story withholds?
Explain "situational irony" using this story's ending as the example.
The whole story in two sentences, without naming the twist directly (make someone want to read it).

L7.12.write: Write a paragraph (5–7 sentences): explain how the phone-call detail in paragraph 2 ("called on Sundays... entirely full") is doing double duty — it establishes the surface story AND plants the clue the ending depends on. Use figurative language, tone, and irony correctly at least once each.
check: Compare your answers with the model answer.
Could you name a specific figurative-language example, correctly state the tone, and state the irony precisely (not just "it was surprising") without rereading?

L7.13.title: Literary Reading II: Unreliable Narrator & Poetry
L7.13.goal: Recognize when a first-person narrator's account of events can't be fully trusted, and read a short poem for figurative meaning, sound, and compression (saying a lot in very few words).

vocab.def: a first-person narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt — because they're lying, mistaken, mentally unwell, a child who doesn't understand what they're describing, or simply too invested in their own version of events to see it clearly. The reader has to read around the narrator's claims to reconstruct what's probably really true
the feelings and associations a word carries beyond its literal dictionary meaning
examples: Slender

facts: first-person narration is never a neutral camera — every narrator selects, frames, and sometimes distorts what they report, whether or not they mean to.
poetry compresses meaning into very few words on purpose; a single concrete image is often doing the work a whole paragraph of abstract explanation would do in prose.
prime.question: recall a time a friend told you their side of an argument they'd had with someone else — did anything in how they told it make you suspect there was more to the other person's side than they were letting on?

text.title: An original short story with an unreliable narrator
paragraphs: A Perfectly Reasonable Explanation

I want to be clear from the start that I am an extremely calm person, and that everything I did that Thursday was completely reasonable given the circumstances, and I would like whoever reads this to keep that firmly in mind, because I know how it's going to sound.

My neighbor, Mr. Feldt, had for several weeks been leaving his garbage bins out on the curb a full day early, which is, if you consult the homeowners' association bylaws — and I have, twice — a clear violation, and which I mentioned to him on four separate occasions, each time perfectly calmly, using a completely normal tone of voice that in no way could be described as anything but civil.

On the Thursday in question, I noticed the bins out again, a full eighteen hours early, and I want to stress that what I did next was not, as my wife later suggested, "unhinged" — that word is simply not accurate — but was, in fact, the only reasonable response left to a reasonable person who had already tried every reasonable channel. I moved the bins. That is all I did. I moved them, calmly, back onto his own driveway, which took, I will admit, several trips, since apparently four days' worth of garbage bins are heavier than one might expect, and I may have raised my voice slightly at one point when he came out onto his porch, though "screaming," which is the word his porch camera's audio apparently picked up according to the police officer who came by later — purely as a courtesy visit, nothing more — is, again, simply not an accurate description of a person who is completely calm.

The officer asked whether I thought this was, perhaps, an overreaction to a bylaw about garbage bins. I explained, calmly, that he clearly did not understand the full eighteen-day history of the situation, at which point he asked whether "eighteen days" sounded to me like something a calm person would have been counting. I did not think that question was especially relevant, and said so, calmly.
questions: List three specific phrases the narrator uses to insist they are "calm" or "reasonable." Why does a narrator who is genuinely calm rarely need to say so this many times?
