Think question: the narrator never once lies about a fact you can point to (the bins were moved; the officer did come by) — the unreliability is entirely in the interpretation laid on top of true events, not in the events themselves. Why can a narrator be unreliable while still technically telling the truth about every individual fact?

text.title: An original poem
paragraphs: What the Water Keeps
The river does not remember the bridge that used to stand here, only the shape a bridge leaves in how a current has to bend.
My grandmother's kitchen is gone, the house sold, the table sold, but I set my own table crooked in the exact way hers always was —
not from clumsiness. From memory keeping a shape it never named, the way water still turns left at a bridge that isn't there.
questions: Identify the poem's central metaphor. What is being compared to what?

The poem never says "I miss my grandmother" or "grief" directly. What specific image carries that meaning instead, and what does the compression (saying it this way, in so few words) add that a direct statement wouldn't?
Look at the word "crooked" in stanza 2. What connotation does it carry here — clumsy/wrong, or something closer to inherited/loving? How does stanza 3 change your reading of "crooked"?

discuss.prompt: If "A Perfectly Reasonable Explanation" continued for one more paragraph, what would the narrator most likely still be denying?
What's one question you'd ask the narrator directly that they'd almost certainly answer unreliably?
Explain "unreliable narrator" to someone using the specific "eighteen days" detail as your proof.
State the poem's central idea in one sentence without using the word memory.

L7.13.write: Choose one: (a) rewrite the garbage-bin Thursday as a neutral, third-person, reliable news-brief version of events (3–4 sentences) — strip out every unreliable framing word; or (b) write your own 3–4 line poem using one concrete, physical image (not an abstract feeling-word) to carry an emotion, the way "crooked" carries inheritance and love in "What the Water Keeps." Use unreliable narrator or connotation correctly at least once in a short explanation of your choice.
check: In your rewrite, did you remove every self-defense word ("calm," "reasonable") while keeping every actual fact? That's the core skill this session teaches.

L7.14.title: Reading Stamina & Speed; Course Capstone Bridge
L7.14.goal: Practice choosing your reading speed on purpose — skim, scan, or deep-read — and sustain a long stretch of deep reading with comprehension; review the level before the mastery check.

vocab.def: moving quickly over a whole text to get the general shape/gist (what's this about, roughly, and is it worth reading closely?) — not aiming to catch every detail
moving quickly through a text looking for one specific piece of information (a date, a name, a number) — not reading for overall meaning at all
slow, careful, often reread reading, aimed at full comprehension of a dense or important passage — the mode this whole level has mostly used

facts: skilled readers don't read everything at the same speed — they switch gears constantly, often without noticing they're doing it, based on what they actually need from a given text.

sustained reading stamina (staying focused through 30+ minutes of dense text) is a trainable capacity that tends to correlate with reading achievement, even though the exact causal direction is still debated (research/06 §1.10).
prime.question: think of the last time you had to read something long and dense (a manual, a syllabus, an assignment) — did you read the whole thing at one speed, or did your pace change depending on the section?

text.title: Matching speed to purpose
paragraphs: Source — a notice

COMMUNITY POOL — SUMMER HOURS NOTICE. Effective June 15 through Labor Day, the community pool will be open Monday–Friday 6:00 AM–8:00 PM and weekends 8:00 AM–7:00 PM, with the exception of the last Wednesday of each month, when the pool closes at 2:00 PM for scheduled maintenance. Lifeguard-supervised swim lessons run Tuesday and Thursday mornings, 9:00–11:00 AM, ages 5 and up, registration required two weeks in advance at the front desk; drop-in lap swim is available during all lifeguarded hours without registration. The pool will be fully closed July 4th for the community holiday event. Guests are limited to two per member household per visit during peak hours (weekends and weekdays after 4:00 PM); a valid membership card is required for entry at all times, and lost cards may be replaced at the front desk for a $5 fee. Pool rules, including no diving in the shallow end and no glass containers on deck, are posted at the entrance and apply to all visitors regardless of membership status.

text.title: Sustained deep reading
paragraphs: The Weight of a Decision You Didn't Notice Making

Most people, asked to name the biggest decision of their life, reach for the obvious candidates: a marriage, a career change, a move to a new city. Fewer people notice the decisions that were never really decided at all — the ones that accumulated, one unremarkable choice at a time, until a shape had formed that nobody had deliberately drawn.

Consider a habit as ordinary as checking a phone first thing in the morning. No one sits down and decides, formally, "I will now spend the first ninety seconds of every day absorbing whatever notification arrived overnight, before I have had a single unprompted thought of my own." And yet that is, in practice, the decision that gets made, daily, by the simple failure to make any decision at all — the phone is there, reaching for it costs nothing in the moment, and the accumulated cost only becomes visible zoomed out, across a year, in a way no single morning ever reveals.

Behavioral researchers have a name for the gap this exploits: present bias — the well- documented tendency to weigh a cost or benefit happening right now far more heavily than an identical cost or benefit happening later, even when, calculated honestly, the two should carry equal weight. Present bias is not a character flaw unique to distracted people; it is close to a universal feature of how human decision-making works, which is exactly why it is so effectively exploited, deliberately, by the design of anything competing for attention — a notification is engineered to make "later" (finishing the thought you were having, sleeping fully) lose to "now" (checking) every single time the two compete, because the app's success is measured by exactly how often "now" wins.

None of this means the fix is willpower, applied harder, in the moment of temptation — present bias, by definition, is precisely the bias that makes in-the-moment willpower an unreliable defense, since the moment itself is engineered to feel low-stakes. The more durable fix, according to the same research tradition, is structural: decisions made in advance, at a calm moment, that remove the in-the-moment choice altogether — a phone charging outside the bedroom, not a phone charging on the nightstand with a promise not to check it; a specific, scheduled time for messages, not an open-ended "I'll just glance quickly" available at every idle moment. The insight generalizes well past phones: nearly any habit someone describes as a failure of willpower is, on closer inspection, better described as a structural decision that was never made — an environment left to default toward whatever is easiest in the moment, which is rarely the same as whatever the person, asked calmly in advance, would actually choose.

This is, in its own way, exactly the disciplinary-reading lesson this level has spent thirteen sessions building toward, aimed inward instead of outward: the same habit of asking "what's actually driving this outcome — the obvious surface reason, or something structural and less visible underneath it" that a historian applies to a deposition, a scientist applies to a correlation, and a critical reader applies to a headline, applies with equal force to a person's own daily habits, if they're willing to read their own life with the same disciplined skepticism they've just spent this level learning to apply to everyone else's claims.
questions: Why does the passage say in-the-moment willpower is an unreliable fix for present bias specifically?
What structural fix does the passage recommend, and how is it different from "just try harder"?

Think question: the final paragraph explicitly connects this passage back to the whole level's disciplinary-reading habit. Restate that connection in your own words — what single question, learned across Sessions 2–13, does the passage say applies just as well to reading your own life?

discuss.prompt: Name one of your own habits that might be a "structural decision that was never made," in the passage's terms.
What's one structural change (not a willpower change) you could actually make this week?
Explain "present bias" to someone who's never heard the term, using an example other than phones.
The whole passage in two sentences.

L7.14.write: Write a paragraph (5–7 sentences) naming one real structural decision in your own life you'd change, using present bias correctly, and stating specifically what environmental change (not a willpower resolution) would remove the in-the-moment choice.
check: Compare your answers with the model answer.

On stamina: did you complete Section 6's passage in one sustained pass without stopping, and answer Q1–5 with reasonable accuracy from that one read? If you needed to reread most of it, that's useful diagnostic information, not failure — note it, and build toward more sustained daily reading time before attempting longer texts.
